en.gtgr_desc: Teaching a computer my accent, and finding out I don’t spell it the same way twice.
en.gtgr_h3_rules-i-didnt-know-i-had: Rules I didn’t know I had
en.gtgr_p1: Graflect is phonic: you spell what you say. So if a computer knows how I talk, it should be able to write Graflect for me. To find out how close one gets, every Graflect article on this site becomes a test. The computer studies all of my other articles, gets only the English of the one left out, and spells it. Then it’s scored on how many words it spelled the way I did.
en.gtgr_p2: The system has two parts. First, my own words: anything I’ve already written in another article gets spelled the same way again. Second, CMUdict, a pronunciation dictionary of American English, put through my rules: tr is cr, dr is jr, a before n and m is ä, and so on. Two more rules look at the next word: “the” is dhī before a vowel, and “have to” is hæf tü. Right now it spells 92% of my words the way I did.
en.gtgr_p3: Most of that is my own words coming back. CMUdict carries a fifth of it, all on words I’ve only ever written in one article.
en.gtgr_p4: Before any of this, the site’s hand-made Graflect dictionary spelled 69% of my words right. The first version of the system got 85.6%. After that, every miss went into a report, sorted by why it was missed, and each step went after the biggest pile.
en.gtgr_ol1:
• First rules system, 85.6%. 882 misses. Nearly half were CMUdict disagreeing with me, and a quarter were my own words disagreeing with each other.
  • tr-words keep the r, 85.9%. crip, crai, cränzlēt. I had been dropping the r after c.
  • Fixes from the P40 report, 87.5%. “The” before a vowel became its own rule, words I usually leave in Latin stay in Latin, dr keeps its r (jr), and I fixed have, had and think in my articles. Me disagreeing with myself went from 219 to 130.
  • ä, īng, no apostrophes, 88.9%. ä before n and m (can, man, hand), -ing is īng, and no apostrophes inside Graflect words: Graflect is phonic. That took out all 60 apostrophe misses.
  • Proofreading round 1, 90.4%. 178 words where CMUdict and I disagreed, or where I had spelled a word more than one way. I changed 91 of them.
  • Slips, and a bug, 90.8%. grælekt, kībõrdz, and “half” written as have. The bug: a change to the converter had it writing “there” as dh·4, two glyphs where I write one.
  • īngg and the wī glyph, 90.8%. Every -ing gets its g, and w then ī is always the wī glyph. 220 words in my articles changed, but the score barely moved: the converter changed to match at the same time.
  • Another bug, more slips, 91.2%. The converter wrote r and ä as the single rä glyph, which I’ve used once. And seven places broke my own rules for “the” and “have to”.
  • i before a final d, z, n, t or s, 92.2%. The report showed where I write the unstressed vowel as i instead of x: ēdid, srvisiz, gárdin, edit. One rule, 66 more words.
en.gtgr_p5: Differences of a whole sound came down steadily as I proofread. The unstressed vowel didn’t move at all until it got a rule of its own.
en.gtgr_ul1:
• CMUdict ≠ me, 248. 135 of these are still the unstressed vowel, x or i. The rest are real differences in how I talk: dikšin4ī, lēngwijiz, sfīr, práblim.
  • Unknown words, 93. Not in CMUdict, and not in my other articles: pinkies, glyphs, encoders, plushies.
  • Me ≠ me, 51. Words that depend on context (read, use, a as x or ē), and 21 words I usually leave in Latin, like system and program, that I spelled out once.
  • Another CMUdict pronunciation, 48. CMUdict lists a second pronunciation that matches mine (srvisiz, dītēl), but the system takes the first.
  • Structure and context, 34. Lines where I rewrote the sentence instead of transliterating it, and four “the”s before names I kept in Latin.
en.gtgr_ul2:
• “The” is dhx, but dhī before a vowel.
  • “A” is x, and ē when I stress it.
  • “And” is änd, but xnd in set pairs like “cookies and cream”.
  • “Have to” is hæf tü.
  • Every -ing has its g: thīngg, yüzīngg.
  • w then ī is the wī glyph: wī, wīl, wīk.
  • The unstressed vowel is i before a final d, z, n, t or s, and x before l, m and p.
en.gtgr_p6: Next, a small neural network trained on Geniza, my home server, with an Nvidia P40. It learns pronunciation from CMUdict first, then my spellings, and it only gets the words the rules can’t handle: the unknown words, and maybe the vowel. Its first run guessed 65% of dictionary words it had never seen exactly right, and added 39 words to the rules’ score. Now that my articles agree with themselves, it’s time to train it again.
